agent_notes: The Hebrew verse numbering counts the superscription as verse 1, so KJV 20:1 is Hebrew 20:2 and the KJV has 9 verses to the Hebrew 10. I translated the Hebrew verses as they stand.

lamnatseach is glossed 'for the choirmaster/leader' following the traditional sense; the root נצח can also mean 'to be eminent, to excel', and the exact musical office is uncertain. The preposition ל before David is deliberately left ambiguous ('of / for / by / concerning David'); Radak and Ibn Ezra both treat it as 'for the sake of David' or 'about David'.

agent_notes: The verse can be divided two ways: 'LORD, save the king; he answers us' (YLT joins 'the king' to 'save') or 'LORD, save! May the King answer us' (KJV, ASV and BBE follow the accent and break after 'save'; their lowercase 'the king' leaves open who answers). Ibn Ezra (as his preferred reading), Radak and Meiri read the King as God; Malbim has King David answering. The atnach after hoshiah supports the break. I followed the accent: 'O YHWH, save! May the King answer us...' and noted the alternatives in the commentary.

agent_notes: The verbs of vv. 2-6a are jussive-or-imperfect forms with no 'may' in the Hebrew. I rendered them as wishes ('may he answer you') in both layers, as KJV, ASV and BBE do; YLT reads them as plain statements. The context (blessing before battle) and the parallel wish in v. 6b favour the wish.

Rashi's remark that 'God of Jacob' recalls the promise at Haran and Radak's midrash on Jacob's distress (Gen 35:3) are reported as the commentators' claims; I did not check the Talmudic and midrashic attributions Radak cites.

history.note: [consider] Mention Rashi's alternative staging, with the king at home and the army in the field, as a second option for the director. (PS.20.2 Rashi: "שֶׁהָיָה שׁוֹלֵחַ אֶת יוֹאָב ... וְהוּא הָיָה עוֹמֵד בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם וּמִתְפַּלֵּל עֲלֵיהֶן".)
[consider] Consider 'from Zion, where his ark rests' or simply 'from Zion'. (PS.20.3 Radak: "והוא הבית שהיה שם הארון".)

agent_notes: yedashsheneh is read as 'turn to ash / find fat and rich (acceptable)', from דשן. The five English versions split: KJV 'accept', YLT 'reduce to ashes', BBE 'be pleased with the fat'. I kept the literal 'make fat / reduce to ash' in layer 1 and 'accept' in the drama. The STEPBible gloss 'may he accept' is too far from the root, so I corrected it. The ending -eh is irregular (Ibn Ezra and Radak compare 've'ekra'ah' in 1 Sam 28:15).
Selah is left as a transliterated word in layer 1 and as a pause in the dramatic layer, since its meaning is unknown.

agent_notes: nidgol: STEPBible and the five versions agree on 'raise a banner' (דגל). Rashi connects it to Ps 60:14 (KJV 60:12), glossing it 'we gather and become an army', as quoted in the packet; I did not check the cited verse myself. The Tiberian pointing of 'beshuatekha' (with a reading mark) is a cantillation matter and does not change the sense.

agent_notes: The speaker changes at 'now I know': a single voice, singular ('I know') after the plural wishes. Ibn Ezra takes it as the psalmist speaking in the Holy Spirit, Radak as each Israelite, Malbim as the head of the singers. I left it open in the translation.
meshicho 'his anointed' is rendered literally. BBE 'his king' interprets. A messianic reading is mentioned by Ibn Ezra, who also allows David; I did not add either reading to the translation layers.

agent_notes: The verb nazkir (hiphil of זכר) lacks an object: 'we cause to be remembered / we invoke'. The five versions split: KJV 'remember', ASV 'make mention', YLT 'make mention', BBE 'we will be strong in' (a paraphrase). I chose 'we make mention' in layer 1, with no object, as YLT and ASV do. Rashi links it to the incense and prayer sense of the hiphil (Is 66:3, Lev 2:2). 'In the chariotry / in the horses' has no verb; the 'trust' of the KJV is supplied from context, and I put it in brackets in layer 1.

agent_notes: The Hebrew word-initial form in 'kamnu' carries a dagesh (קַּמְנוּ) that STEPBible keeps; I treat it as the ordinary perfect 'we rose', not a separate verb. The last verb vanit'odad is a hithpolel of עוד (rooted by STEPBible at H5749A); its sense 'we were set upright / we stood firm' is standard and Rashi ties it to 'me'oded anavim' in Ps 147:6.
